from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
text=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 t=p.extract_text()
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02}.txt').write_text(t)
 text.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(text))
print(''.join(text[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper identifies a useful retrieval setting: combining a reference person image with a relative description without training on composed-query triplets. ITCPR provides a potentially valuable evaluation resource, with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery assembled from three existing datasets.

The reported improvements over simple fusion are substantial and consistent across two backbones. With ViT-L/14, even the single text-supervised TINet achieves 45.55% Rank-1 and 55.26% mAP, versus 32.02% and 41.83% for image–text averaging with the same fine-tuned encoders.

The experimental analysis covers visual versus textual supervision, CMPM versus instance-level contrastive learning, network architecture, prompt templates, token length, training-data volume, and ensemble efficiency. The pseudo-word replacement experiment also provides useful evidence that the learned representation captures more information than its nearest vocabulary word.

The two-stage framework is understandable and practical. Freezing the encoders during inversion-network training limits optimization costs, and the manuscript supplies substantial implementation information, including learning rates, batch size, training duration, network dimensions, and hardware.
weaknesses: The central comparison with prior textual-inversion methods is confounded. Table 1 pairs Pic2Word and SEARLE mappings trained with original CLIP with fine-tuned encoders, whereas Word4Per trains its mapping in the adapted representation space using person-domain data. This introduces both training-data and representation-mismatch disadvantages. Table B provides a useful partial control, but its visual ITC-to-CMPM improvement is approximately 3.13 percentage points, substantially smaller than the headline comparison. Matched retraining of the competing methods is needed to establish the claimed methodological advantage.

The evaluation does not clearly separate model selection from testing. ITCPR is explicitly designated exclusively for testing, yet Section 5.3 selects architecture and prompt configurations using performance on this benchmark. No independent development protocol is described. Avoiding CPR triplets during gradient training does not eliminate the potential optimism introduced by selecting configurations on the test set.

Methodological originality is limited relative to the framing. Mapping image features into pseudo-word embeddings and composing them through a frozen text encoder closely follows Pic2Word and SEARLE; encoder adaptation and the component losses also derive from established work. The task and benchmark are meaningful contributions, but the manuscript should more precisely distinguish those contributions from the incremental changes to the retrieval method.

The benchmark needs stronger validation and documentation. Appendix B.1 screens potential missing positives using an unspecified visual encoder and an unspecified top-k cutoff, without measuring remaining annotation errors. Annotator agreement and results separated by source dataset or modification type are absent. Since all CPR results depend on this single newly constructed benchmark, these omissions limit confidence in both annotation completeness and generality. Uncertainty estimates would also help assess the smaller ablation gains.

Some details affecting reproducibility remain ambiguous. Table 1 describes the combined visual/textual condition as loss supervision, while Appendix C.4 associates those results with fusion of separately trained TINets. Joint-loss training and inference-time ensembling should be distinguished explicitly, including their configurations and computational costs.

The proposed dataset and application involve identifiable people and retrieval across clothing changes, yet the manuscript does not document reuse permissions or discuss privacy and potential nonconsensual tracking. These are relevant ethical reporting gaps for the stated security application.
